claim: The proteostasis network has evolved to support protein folding under normal conditions and to expand this capacity in response to proteotoxic stresses.
source: The proteostasis network has evolved to support protein folding under normal conditions and to expand this capacity in response to proteotoxic stresses.
evidence: This is a general statement about the proteostasis network that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Many pathogenic states are associated with protein misfolding, revealing in vivo limitations on quality control mechanisms.
source: Nevertheless, many pathogenic states are associated with protein misfolding, revealing in vivo limitations on quality control mechanisms.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about the relationship between protein misfolding and disease.

claim: Amyloids are largely resistant to clearance.
source: One contributor to these limitations is the physical characteristics of misfolded proteins, as exemplified by amyloids, which are largely resistant to clearance.
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of amyloids in the scientific literature.

claim: Sup35 amyloid is disassembled at elevated temperatures by the molecular chaperone Hsp104.
source: Remarkably, Sup35 amyloid is disassembled at elevated temperatures by the molecular chaperone Hsp104.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Hsp104-mediated disassembly of Sup35 amyloid requires Hsp104 engagement with heat-induced non-prion aggregates in late cell-cycle stage cells.
source: This process requires Hsp104 engagement with heat-induced non-prion aggregates in late cell-cycle stage cells, which promotes its asymmetric retention and thereby effective activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 4, 5, 6, and 7.

claim: Cell division imposes a potent limitation on proteostasis capacity.
source: Thus, cell division imposes a potent limitation on proteostasis capacity that can be bypassed by the spatial engagement of a quality control factor.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: The PQC network can adapt when buffering thresholds are exceeded by elevating the expression of PQC factors.
source: The PQC network is tailored to buffer protein folding in a distinct homeostatic niche but can adapt when these buffering thresholds are exceeded by elevating the expression of PQC factors, including proteases and molecular chaperones, to clear accumulating misfolded proteins (Morimoto, 2008; Powers et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In cases such as thermal stress, PQC corrections are sufficient to restore balance.
source: In cases such as thermal stress, these corrections are sufficient to restore balance, but in others such as aging, misfolded proteins assemble into ordered amyloid aggregates, which persist and dramatically alter cellular physiology by inducing disease (Tuite and Serio, 2010; Voisine et al., 2010; Taylor and Dillin, 2011; Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In aging, misfolded proteins assemble into ordered amyloid aggregates, which persist and dramatically alter cellular physiology by inducing disease.
source: In cases such as thermal stress, these corrections are sufficient to restore balance, but in others such as aging, misfolded proteins assemble into ordered amyloid aggregates, which persist and dramatically alter cellular physiology by inducing disease (Tuite and Serio, 2010; Voisine et al., 2010; Taylor and Dillin, 2011; Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Proteostasis collapse has been linked to the unique ability of amyloids to incorporate and conformationally convert like protein to the misfolded state and to their high thermodynamic stability.
source: This proteostasis collapse has been linked to the unique ability of amyloids to incorporate and conformationally convert like protein to the misfolded state and to their high thermodynamic stability (Chiti and Dobson, 2006; Jahn and Radford, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The properties of amyloids are thought to enhance the production and restrict the resolution of the misfolded protein to the point that the buffering capacity and adaptability of the proteostasis network is chronically exceeded.
source: Together, these properties are thought to enhance the production and restrict the resolution of the misfolded protein to the point that the buffering capacity and adaptability of the proteostasis network is chronically exceeded.
evidence: This is a statement about the prevailing understanding in the field, based on inference from known properties of amyloids.

claim: Heterologous overexpression of molecular chaperones in C. elegans, mice, Drosophila, yeast, and tissue culture-cell models of amyloidoses reduces proteotoxicity.
source: Despite this natural upper boundary on proteostasis capacity, the heterologous overexpression of molecular chaperones in Caenorhabditis elegans, mice, Drosophila, yeast, and tissue culture-cell models of amyloidoses reduces proteotoxicity (Chernoff et al., 1995; Morimoto, 2008; Broadley and Hartl, 2009; Holmes et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Existing protein has not been demonstrated to transition from an amyloid to a non-amyloid form in studies of chaperone overexpression.
source: While these observations are often interpreted as evidence of amyloid resolution, existing protein has not been demonstrated to transition from an amyloid to a non-amyloid form in any of the studies.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from a review of the literature on chaperone overexpression studies.

claim: In cases where the mechanism has been determined, the reduction in amyloid accumulation results from an inhibition of amyloid assembly by the overexpressed chaperone.
source: In the few cases where the mechanism has been determined, the reduction in amyloid accumulation results from an inhibition of amyloid assembly by the overexpressed chaperone (Kobayashi et al., 2000; Schaffar et al., 2004; Tam et al., 2006; Shorter and Lindquist, 2008; Winkler et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Even the specific overexpression of individual chaperones is unable to extend the proteostasis upper boundary in vivo to resolve protein amyloids.
source: Thus, even the specific overexpression of individual chaperones is unable to extend the proteostasis upper boundary in vivo to resolve protein amyloids.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the review of literature on chaperone overexpression.

claim: Repressing expression of an amyloidogenic protein can reverse established toxicity and, at least in some cases, clear existing amyloid.
source: For example, repressing expression of an amyloidogenic protein can reverse established toxicity and, at least in some cases, clear existing amyloid (Yamamoto et al., 2000; Mallucci et al., 2003; Lim et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Expression of a dominant-negative mutant promotes disassembly of wild-type amyloid in vivo.
source: In addition, expression of a dominant-negative mutant also promotes disassembly of wild-type amyloid in vivo (DiSalvo et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Amyloid clearance mechanisms exist in vivo.
source: Together, these observations suggest that amyloid clearance mechanisms exist in vivo, and indeed amyloid resolution is biochemically feasible in vitro using purified chaperones such as yeast Hsp104, alone or in combination with its co-chaperones Hsp40, Hsp70, and small heat shock proteins (Inoue et al., 2004; Shorter and Lindquist, 2004, Lo Bianco et al., 2008; Shorter and Lindquist, 2008).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Amyloid resolution is biochemically feasible in vitro using purified chaperones such as yeast Hsp104, alone or in combination with its co-chaperones Hsp40, Hsp70, and small heat shock proteins.
source: Together, these observations suggest that amyloid clearance mechanisms exist in vivo, and indeed amyloid resolution is biochemically feasible in vitro using purified chaperones such as yeast Hsp104, alone or in combination with its co-chaperones Hsp40, Hsp70, and small heat shock proteins (Inoue et al., 2004; Shorter and Lindquist, 2004, Lo Bianco et al., 2008; Shorter and Lindquist, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: [PSI+] is the alternative, self-templating, amyloid form of the Sup35 protein.
source: To identify cell-based limitations on proteostasis capacity, we focused on the mechanisms controlling persistence of the yeast prion [PSI+], the alternative, self-templating, amyloid form of the Sup35 protein (Cox, 1965; Patino et al., 1996; Paushkin et al., 1996; Glover et al., 1997; King et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Under normal growth conditions, [PSI+] propagates faithfully.
source: Under normal growth conditions, [PSI+] propagates faithfully (Cox, 1965; Derkatch et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: At elevated temperatures where the PQC capacity is increased, [PSI+] becomes destabilized in a Sup35 conformation-specific manner.
source: However, at elevated temperatures where the PQC capacity is increased, [PSI+] becomes destabilized in a Sup35 conformation-specific manner.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and data in Figure 1.

claim: The more thermodynamically stable but less efficiently propagated [PSI+]Weak variant is quantitatively 'cured' at elevated temperature in comparison with [PSI+]Strong.
source: For example, the more thermodynamically stable but less efficiently propagated [PSI+]Weak variant is quantitatively 'cured' (i.e. converted to the non-prion [psi−] state) at elevated temperature in comparison with [PSI+]Strong, whose propagation is unaltered under the same conditions (Cox et al., 1988; Derkatch et al., 1996; Jung et al., 2000; Tanaka et al., 2006; Newnam et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and data in Figure 1.

claim: [PSI+]Strong propagation is unaltered at elevated temperature.
source: For example, the more thermodynamically stable but less efficiently propagated [PSI+]Weak variant is quantitatively 'cured' (i.e. converted to the non-prion [psi−] state) at elevated temperature in comparison with [PSI+]Strong, whose propagation is unaltered under the same conditions (Cox et al., 1988; Derkatch et al., 1996; Jung et al., 2000; Tanaka et al., 2006; Newnam et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and data in Figure 1A.

claim: Curing of [PSI+]Weak was linked to the inhibition of the molecular chaperone Hsp104.
source: This curing of [PSI+]Weak was linked to the inhibition of the molecular chaperone Hsp104 (Newnam et al., 2011), an observation that is seemingly counter to the idea that proteostasis capacity increases in response to stress (Morimoto, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Stationary phase alters chaperone expression and blocks [PSI+] curing at elevated temperature.
source: Because stationary phase alters chaperone expression and blocks [PSI+] curing at elevated temperature (Gasch et al., 2000; Newnam et al., 2011), residual effects from the growth phase switch could alter the interaction between Sup35 aggregates and PQC factors.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Transiently elevating the growth temperature from 30°C to 40°C had no effect on viability.
source: Transiently elevating the growth temperature from 30°C to 40°C had no effect on viability (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) or on [PSI+]Strong propagation (Figure 1A) but induced [PSI+]Weak curing (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Transiently elevating the growth temperature from 30°C to 40°C had no effect on [PSI+]Strong propagation.
source: Transiently elevating the growth temperature from 30°C to 40°C had no effect on viability (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) or on [PSI+]Strong propagation (Figure 1A) but induced [PSI+]Weak curing (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Transiently elevating the growth temperature from 30°C to 40°C induced [PSI+]Weak curing.
source: Transiently elevating the growth temperature from 30°C to 40°C had no effect on viability (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) or on [PSI+]Strong propagation (Figure 1A) but induced [PSI+]Weak curing (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1A and 1B.

claim: Both fully red and sectored colonies were observed following thermal stress, indicating that curing happened during both the thermal stress and subsequent recovery.
source: Notably, both fully red and sectored colonies were observed, indicating that curing happened during both the thermal stress and subsequent recovery (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 1B, with an inference about the timing of curing.

claim: [PSI+]Weak propagation is similarly sensitive to elevated temperature in exponentially growing cultures and in those that have recently exited stationary phase.
source: Thus, [PSI+]Weak propagation is similarly sensitive to elevated temperature in exponentially growing cultures and in those that have recently exited stationary phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the current study's results with previous literature.

claim: At the normal growth temperature, large Sup35 aggregates are fragmented into smaller complexes by Hsp104.
source: At the normal growth temperature, large Sup35 aggregates are fragmented into smaller complexes by Hsp104 (Chernoff et al., 1995; Eaglestone et al., 2000; Ness et al., 2002; Satpute-Krishnan et al., 2007; Kawai-Noma et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In a culture that recently exited stationary phase, the size of SDS-resistant Sup35 aggregates increased following incubation at 40°C and a 2 hr recovery at 30°C.
source: In a culture that recently exited stationary phase, the size of SDS-resistant Sup35 aggregates increased, as assessed by semi-denaturing detergent agarose gel electrophoresis (SDD-AGE) (Kryndushkin et al., 2003), following incubation at 40°C and a 2 hr recovery at 30°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, left) (Newnam et al., 2011), consistent with an inhibition of fragmentation (Newnam et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and citations to previous literature.

claim: SDS-resistant Sup35 aggregates were immediately reduced in size following thermal treatment of an exponentially growing [PSI+]Weak strain.
source: In contrast, SDS-resistant Sup35 aggregates were immediately reduced in size (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and completely lost after recovery (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, right) following identical treatment of an exponentially growing [PSI+]Weak strain, a progression suggesting the resolution of existing Sup35 aggregates.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: SDS-resistant Sup35 aggregates were completely lost after recovery following thermal treatment of an exponentially growing [PSI+]Weak strain.
source: In contrast, SDS-resistant Sup35 aggregates were immediately reduced in size (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and completely lost after recovery (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, right) following identical treatment of an exponentially growing [PSI+]Weak strain, a progression suggesting the resolution of existing Sup35 aggregates.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Over 70% of SDS-resistant Sup35 became detergent sensitive during recovery at 30°C following incubation at 40°C.
source: However, following incubation at 40°C, over 70% of SDS-resistant Sup35 became detergent sensitive during recovery at 30°C (Figure 1D), indicating disassembly of existing Sup35 amyloid.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The transition of SDS-resistant Sup35 to an SDS-sensitive state indicates disassembly of existing Sup35 amyloid.
source: However, following incubation at 40°C, over 70% of SDS-resistant Sup35 became detergent sensitive during recovery at 30°C (Figure 1D), indicating disassembly of existing Sup35 amyloid.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Chemical inhibition of Hsp104 with GdnHCl treatment reduced [PSI+]Weak curing by more than 50% relative to the wild-type untreated strain.
source: To determine if the prion curing resulting from this disassembly was mediated by Hsp104, we chemically inhibited this factor with guanidine HCl (GdnHCl) treatment or reduced its dosage by creating a heterozygous disruption in a diploid strain (Eaglestone et al., 1999; Jung and Masison, 2001; Grimminger et al., 2004; Kummer et al., 2013; Tariq et al., 2013; Zeymer et al., 2013), and in both cases, [PSI+]Weak curing was reduced by more than 50% relative to the wild-type untreated strain (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Reducing Hsp104 dosage by creating a heterozygous disruption in a diploid strain reduced [PSI+]Weak curing by more than 50% relative to the wild-type untreated strain.
source: To determine if the prion curing resulting from this disassembly was mediated by Hsp104, we chemically inhibited this factor with guanidine HCl (GdnHCl) treatment or reduced its dosage by creating a heterozygous disruption in a diploid strain (Eaglestone et al., 1999; Jung and Masison, 2001; Grimminger et al., 2004; Kummer et al., 2013; Tariq et al., 2013; Zeymer et al., 2013), and in both cases, [PSI+]Weak curing was reduced by more than 50% relative to the wild-type untreated strain (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Hsp104 promotes the disassembly of existing Sup35 amyloid in a [PSI+]Weak strain following thermal stress.
source: Thus, Hsp104 promotes the disassembly of existing Sup35 amyloid in a [PSI+]Weak strain following thermal stress.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The size of SDS-resistant Sup35 aggregates is reduced in a [PSI+]Strong strain at elevated temperature.
source: At elevated temperature, we noted that the size of SDS-resistant Sup35 aggregates is reduced in a [PSI+]Strong strain (Figure 1C), although curing does not occur (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: [PSI+]Strong is not cured at elevated temperature despite a reduction in aggregate size.
source: At elevated temperature, we noted that the size of SDS-resistant Sup35 aggregates is reduced in a [PSI+]Strong strain (Figure 1C), although curing does not occur (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: [PSI+]Strong propagates more efficiently than [PSI+]Weak.
source: Because [PSI+]Strong propagates more efficiently than [PSI+]Weak, the former may be protected from curing at elevated temperature if the rate of Sup35 assembly continued to outpace the rate of its disassembly, a scenario that should be reversed by reducing the efficiency of [PSI+]Strong propagation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the two prion variants, supported by citations elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: Expressing a Sup35 mutant (G58D) in a [PSI+]Strong diploid strain promotes curing at elevated temperature.
source: To test this idea, we subjected [PSI+]Strong diploid strains heterozygous for either a Sup35 mutant (G58D) or for a Sup35 disruption, which both reduce propagation efficiency (Derdowski et al., 2010; DiSalvo et al., 2011), to thermal stress. At 30°C, [PSI+] propagation is stable in both of these strains (Figure 2C,D); however at 40°C, both were now efficiently cured (e.g. ∼100% for WT/G58D, ∼60% for SUP35/Δ) (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Decreasing the expression of wild-type Sup35 in a [PSI+]Strong diploid strain promotes curing at elevated temperature.
source: To test this idea, we subjected [PSI+]Strong diploid strains heterozygous for either a Sup35 mutant (G58D) or for a Sup35 disruption, which both reduce propagation efficiency (Derdowski et al., 2010; DiSalvo et al., 2011), to thermal stress. At 30°C, [PSI+] propagation is stable in both of these strains (Figure 2C,D); however at 40°C, both were now efficiently cured (e.g. ∼100% for WT/G58D, ∼60% for SUP35/Δ) (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Exposure to 40°C induced quantitative [PSI+]Weak curing.
source: For example, while exposure to 40°C induced quantitative [PSI+]Weak curing, pretreatment at 37°C prior to exposure to 40°C slightly reduced curing (Figure 1A,B, compare proportion of fully cured colonies), and incubation at 37°C did not induce curing at all (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1A and 1B.

claim: Pretreatment at 37°C prior to exposure to 40°C slightly reduced [PSI+]Weak curing.
source: For example, while exposure to 40°C induced quantitative [PSI+]Weak curing, pretreatment at 37°C prior to exposure to 40°C slightly reduced curing (Figure 1A,B, compare proportion of fully cured colonies), and incubation at 37°C did not induce curing at all (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1A and 1B.

claim: Incubation at 37°C did not induce [PSI+]Weak curing.
source: For example, while exposure to 40°C induced quantitative [PSI+]Weak curing, pretreatment at 37°C prior to exposure to 40°C slightly reduced curing (Figure 1A,B, compare proportion of fully cured colonies), and incubation at 37°C did not induce curing at all (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1A and 1B.

claim: The failure to destabilize [PSI+]Weak at 37°C corresponded to an increase in aggregate size relative to growth at 40°C alone.
source: This failure to destabilize [PSI+]Weak at 37°C corresponded to an increase in aggregate size (Figure 1C) and a decrease in Sup35 solubilization (Figure 1D) relative to growth at 40°C alone, indicating a temperature-dependent modulation of amyloid resolution.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The failure to destabilize [PSI+]Weak at 37°C corresponded to a decrease in Sup35 solubilization relative to growth at 40°C alone.
source: This failure to destabilize [PSI+]Weak at 37°C corresponded to an increase in aggregate size (Figure 1C) and a decrease in Sup35 solubilization (Figure 1D) relative to growth at 40°C alone, indicating a temperature-dependent modulation of amyloid resolution.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Neither Sup35 nor chaperone levels correlated with curing efficiency.
source: By quantitative immunoblotting, neither Sup35 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) nor chaperone levels (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) correlated with curing efficiency (Figure 1A), indicating that [PSI+]Weak curing could not be explained by simple changes in protein expression.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: [PSI+]Weak curing could not be explained by simple changes in protein expression.
source: By quantitative immunoblotting, neither Sup35 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) nor chaperone levels (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) correlated with curing efficiency (Figure 1A), indicating that [PSI+]Weak curing could not be explained by simple changes in protein expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Specific overexpression of Hsp104 alone from a galactose-inducible promoter to levels that parallel those achieved during thermal stress induces ∼40% [PSI+]Weak curing.
source: Indeed, the specific overexpression of Hsp104 alone from a galactose-inducible promoter to levels that parallel those achieved during thermal stress (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) induces ∼40% [PSI+]Weak curing (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, 1.5 gen) in comparison with the ∼95% [PSI+]Weak curing induced by thermal stress (Figure 1B) (DiSalvo et al., 2011, Wegrzyn et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and citations to previous literature.

claim: Thermal stress induces ∼95% [PSI+]Weak curing.
source: Indeed, the specific overexpression of Hsp104 alone from a galactose-inducible promoter to levels that parallel those achieved during thermal stress (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) induces ∼40% [PSI+]Weak curing (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, 1.5 gen) in comparison with the ∼95% [PSI+]Weak curing induced by thermal stress (Figure 1B) (DiSalvo et al., 2011, Wegrzyn et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Hsp104 overexpression alone leads to an increase in the size of SDS-resistant Sup35 aggregates isolated from a [PSI+]Weak strain.
source: Moreover, Hsp104 overexpression alone leads to an increase in the size of SDS-resistant Sup35 aggregates isolated from a [PSI+]Weak strain (Kryndushkin et al., 2003), as previously reported for [PSI+]Strong (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) (Kryndushkin et al., 2003), but this outcome is in obvious contrast to the disassembly of Sup35 amyloid that we observe upon thermal stress (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and a citation to previous literature.

claim: Thermal stress and chaperone overexpression induce distinct changes in prion propagation.
source: Thus, thermal stress and chaperone overexpression induce distinct changes in prion propagation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the effects of thermal stress and Hsp104 overexpression on Sup35 aggregates.

claim: Protein aggregates accumulated independent of prion status at all elevated temperatures.
source: By differential centrifugation, protein aggregates accumulated independent of prion status at all elevated temperatures (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), but in contrast to chaperone expression (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), the severity of this accumulation was impacted by growth temperature.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The severity of protein aggregate accumulation was impacted by growth temperature.
source: By differential centrifugation, protein aggregates accumulated independent of prion status at all elevated temperatures (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), but in contrast to chaperone expression (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), the severity of this accumulation was impacted by growth temperature.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At 37°C, protein aggregation increased by less than 10% in comparison with a culture maintained at 30°C.
source: At 37°C, protein aggregation increased by less than 10% in comparison with a culture maintained at 30°C (Figure 3B, column 1), but in cultures treated at 37°C followed by 40°C or directly at 40°C, this level rose to ∼20% or ∼40%, respectively (Figure 3B, columns 3 and 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In cultures treated at 37°C followed by 40°C, protein aggregation increased to ∼20%.
source: At 37°C, protein aggregation increased by less than 10% in comparison with a culture maintained at 30°C (Figure 3B, column 1), but in cultures treated at 37°C followed by 40°C or directly at 40°C, this level rose to ∼20% or ∼40%, respectively (Figure 3B, columns 3 and 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In cultures treated directly at 40°C, protein aggregation increased to ∼40%.
source: At 37°C, protein aggregation increased by less than 10% in comparison with a culture maintained at 30°C (Figure 3B, column 1), but in cultures treated at 37°C followed by 40°C or directly at 40°C, this level rose to ∼20% or ∼40%, respectively (Figure 3B, columns 3 and 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The accumulation of protein aggregates correlates directly with curing efficiency at the various temperatures.
source: Thus, the accumulation of protein aggregates (Figure 3B) correlates directly with curing efficiency at the various temperatures (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing data in Figure 3B with Figure 1A.

claim: GdnHCl treatment during a 40°C incubation strongly reduced curing efficiency but did not reduce the accumulation of protein aggregates.
source: We noted, however, that this correlation was not observed for a [PSI+]Weak culture treated with GdnHCl during a 40°C incubation, which strongly reduced curing efficiency (Figure 2A) but did not reduce the accumulation of protein aggregates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: GdnHCl blocks the association of Hsp104 with at least one substrate.
source: Nevertheless, numerous studies have reported the localization of chaperones to cytoplasmic quality control foci upon exposure to proteotoxic stresses (Aguilaniu et al., 2003; Erjavec et al., 2007; Kaganovich et al., 2008; Specht et al., 2011; Wolfe et al., 2013), and GdnHCl blocks the association of Hsp104 with at least one substrate (Winkler et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Chaperones localize to cytoplasmic quality control foci upon exposure to proteotoxic stresses.
source: Nevertheless, numerous studies have reported the localization of chaperones to cytoplasmic quality control foci upon exposure to proteotoxic stresses (Aguilaniu et al., 2003; Erjavec et al., 2007; Kaganovich et al., 2008; Specht et al., 2011; Wolfe et al., 2013), and GdnHCl blocks the association of Hsp104 with at least one substrate (Winkler et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: At elevated temperatures, there is an increase in Hsp104-interacting proteins as assessed by co-immunocapture.
source: At elevated temperatures, we observed an increase Hsp104-interacting proteins as assessed by co-immunocapture (Figure 4A) and the localization of Hsp104-GFP to cytoplasmic foci (Figure 4B,C), which also contain the model substrate firefly luciferase-mCherry (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Hsp104-GFP localizes to cytoplasmic foci at elevated temperatures.
source: At elevated temperatures, we observed an increase Hsp104-interacting proteins as assessed by co-immunocapture (Figure 4A) and the localization of Hsp104-GFP to cytoplasmic foci (Figure 4B,C), which also contain the model substrate firefly luciferase-mCherry (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: Hsp104-GFP cytoplasmic foci contain the model substrate firefly luciferase-mCherry.
source: At elevated temperatures, we observed an increase Hsp104-interacting proteins as assessed by co-immunocapture (Figure 4A) and the localization of Hsp104-GFP to cytoplasmic foci (Figure 4B,C), which also contain the model substrate firefly luciferase-mCherry (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The amount of co-immunocaptured proteins and the number and intensity of Hsp104-GFP fluorescent foci corresponded to both the accumulation of heat-induced protein aggregates and the efficiency of curing.
source: The amount of co-immunocaptured proteins (Figure 4A [2.5-fold increase at 37°C and 4.2-fold increase at 40°C relative to 30°C]) and the number and intensity of Hsp104-GFP fluorescent foci (Figure 4C) corresponded to both the accumulation of heat-induced protein aggregates (Figure 3B) and the efficiency of curing (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing data in Figures 4A, 4C, 3B, and 1A.

claim: The Hsp104-GFP fluorescence pattern was unaltered in a non-prion [psi−] strain.
source: Notably, the Hsp104-GFP fluorescence pattern was unaltered in a non-prion [psi−] strain (Figure 4B), indicating that Hsp104-GFP was engaged with non-prion substrates.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Hsp104-GFP was engaged with non-prion substrates at elevated temperature.
source: Notably, the Hsp104-GFP fluorescence pattern was unaltered in a non-prion [psi−] strain (Figure 4B), indicating that Hsp104-GFP was engaged with non-prion substrates.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Hsp104-GFP localization is similar in [PSI+] and [psi−] strains, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Treatment of a [PSI+]Weak culture with GdnHCl during an incubation at 40°C strongly reduces Hsp104-GFP association with heat-induced interacting proteins.
source: Treatment of a [PSI+]Weak culture with GdnHCl during an incubation at 40°C, which strongly reduces Hsp104-GFP association with heat-induced interacting proteins (Figure 4A [1.7-fold decrease relative to 40°C in the absence of GdnHCl]) and localization to cytoplasmic foci (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), also reduces the efficiency of curing (Figure 2A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Treatment of a [PSI+]Weak culture with GdnHCl during an incubation at 40°C reduces Hsp104-GFP localization to cytoplasmic foci.
source: Treatment of a [PSI+]Weak culture with GdnHCl during an incubation at 40°C, which strongly reduces Hsp104-GFP association with heat-induced interacting proteins (Figure 4A [1.7-fold decrease relative to 40°C in the absence of GdnHCl]) and localization to cytoplasmic foci (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), also reduces the efficiency of curing (Figure 2A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The specific engagement of Hsp104 with heat-induced aggregates, rather than simply their presence, correlates with curing at elevated temperature.
source: Thus, the specific engagement of Hsp104 with heat-induced aggregates, rather than simply their presence, correlates with curing at elevated temperature.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings shown in Figures 2A, 4A, and 4—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: The asymmetric localization of Hsp104 results from its engagement with heat-induced protein aggregates.
source: One possibility is that the asymmetric localization of Hsp104, resulting from its engagement with heat-induced protein aggregates (Erjavec et al., 2007), increases its accumulation in a subpopulation of cells beyond that which can be achieved by its transcriptional up-regulation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation to previous literature and tested in the subsequent experiments.

claim: Mother cells accumulated ∼60% of Hsp104-GFP following the completion of cell division at 30°C.
source: Starting with budded cells, mother cells accumulated ∼60% of Hsp104-GFP following the completion of cell division at 30°C (Figure 5A, gray), which is comparable to the accumulation of untagged GFP expressed from the same promoter (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and thus likely reflects the volume differences between mother and daughter cells.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The baseline asymmetry of Hsp104-GFP progressively increased as the temperature was increased.
source: This baseline asymmetry progressively increased as the temperature was increased to 37°C (∼65% retention), 37°C followed by 40°C (∼73% retention), and finally 40°C (∼75% retention; Figure 5A, gray).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Both Ssa1-GFP and Sis1-GFP fusions localized to cytoplasmic foci.
source: Notably, both Ssa1-GFP and Sis1-GFP fusions also localized to cytoplasmic, and, in the case of Sis1, nuclear foci (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C), but neither was asymmetrically retained following incubation at 40°C (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E), although their levels were elevated relative to 30°C (Table 1) due to their enhanced expression (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Sis1-GFP localized to nuclear foci.
source: Notably, both Ssa1-GFP and Sis1-GFP fusions also localized to cytoplasmic, and, in the case of Sis1, nuclear foci (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C), but neither was asymmetrically retained following incubation at 40°C (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E), although their levels were elevated relative to 30°C (Table 1) due to their enhanced expression (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Neither Ssa1-GFP nor Sis1-GFP was asymmetrically retained following incubation at 40°C.
source: Notably, both Ssa1-GFP and Sis1-GFP fusions also localized to cytoplasmic, and, in the case of Sis1, nuclear foci (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C), but neither was asymmetrically retained following incubation at 40°C (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E), although their levels were elevated relative to 30°C (Table 1) due to their enhanced expression (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: Curing efficiency correlates directly with the asymmetric retention of Hsp104 in cells at elevated temperature.
source: Thus, curing efficiency (Figure 1A,B) correlates directly with the asymmetric retention of Hsp104 in cells at elevated temperature.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing data in Figures 1A,B and 5A.

claim: Disruption of the formin BNI1 did not alter Hsp104 expression levels or the accumulation of protein aggregates at 30°C and 40°C relative to a wild-type strain.
source: Disruption of the formin BNI1 (Kohno et al., 1996) did not alter Hsp104 expression levels or the accumulation of protein aggregates at 30°C and 40°C relative to a wild-type strain, (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F,G) but, Hsp104 asymmetric retention was reduced (Figure 5B, green), as expected (Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: Disruption of BNI1 reduced Hsp104 asymmetric retention.
source: Disruption of the formin BNI1 (Kohno et al., 1996) did not alter Hsp104 expression levels or the accumulation of protein aggregates at 30°C and 40°C relative to a wild-type strain, (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F,G) but, Hsp104 asymmetric retention was reduced (Figure 5B, green), as expected (Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and a citation to previous literature.

claim: Curing was dramatically suppressed from ∼80% for a wild-type strain to ∼10% in the Δbni1 strain.
source: Strikingly, curing was dramatically suppressed from ∼80% for a wild-type strain to ∼10% in the Δbni1 strain (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: GdnHCl treatment before thermal stress reduced Hsp104-GFP asymmetric retention following exposure to 40°C.
source: Likewise, GdnHCl treatment before thermal stress, which blocked both Hsp104 engagement with heat-induced aggregates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F) and curing at elevated temperature (Figure 2A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G), also reduced Hsp104-GFP asymmetric retention following exposure to 40°C (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The asymmetric retention of Hsp104 is required for curing.
source: Thus, the asymmetric retention of Hsp104 is required for curing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings shown in Figures 5B,C,D.

claim: Mother cells, which experienced the elevated temperature and accumulated Hsp104, were more likely to be cured than their daughters.
source: Mother cells, which experienced the elevated temperature and accumulated Hsp104 (Figure 5A), were more likely to be cured than their daughters (Figure 5E, note most data points fall below the diagonal), as predicted by our hypothesis.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The efficiency of curing correlated directly with the accumulation of Hsp104-GFP.
source: When these subpopulations were separated by FACS and analyzed for colony-based phenotype, the efficiency of curing correlated directly with the accumulation of Hsp104-GFP (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5F and 5G.

claim: Cells exposed to elevated temperature accumulate heat-induced protein aggregates, asymmetrically retain Hsp104 in a manner that is proportional to these substrates, and ultimately cure [PSI+]Weak.
source: Together, these observations indicate that cells exposed to elevated temperature accumulate heat-induced protein aggregates, asymmetrically retain Hsp104 in a manner that is proportional to these substrates, and ultimately cure [PSI+]Weak.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings shown in Figures 3, 4, and 5.

claim: Blocking the ATPase activity of Hsp104 after thermal stress with GdnHCl failed to reduce Hsp104-GFP localization to cytoplasmic foci.
source: Indeed, blocking the ATPase activity of Hsp104 after thermal stress with a 90-min treatment with GdnHCl failed to reduce Hsp104-GFP localization to cytoplasmic foci (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F) or its asymmetric retention (Figure 5D), presumably because the chaperone bound to heat-induced substrates but was unable to release them once inhibited with GdnHCl.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Blocking the ATPase activity of Hsp104 after thermal stress with GdnHCl failed to reduce its asymmetric retention.
source: Indeed, blocking the ATPase activity of Hsp104 after thermal stress with a 90-min treatment with GdnHCl failed to reduce Hsp104-GFP localization to cytoplasmic foci (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F) or its asymmetric retention (Figure 5D), presumably because the chaperone bound to heat-induced substrates but was unable to release them once inhibited with GdnHCl.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Despite the asymmetric localization of Hsp104-GFP when GdnHCl is added after thermal stress, [PSI+]Weak curing was reduced by nearly 50%.
source: Despite the asymmetric localization of Hsp104-GFP under these conditions, [PSI+]Weak curing was reduced by nearly 50% (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Both Hsp104 asymmetric localization and activity are required to induce [PSI+]Weak curing following thermal stress.
source: Thus, both Hsp104 asymmetric localization and activity are required to induce [PSI+]Weak curing following thermal stress.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings shown in Figures 4—figure supplement 1F,G and 5D.

claim: Treatment with α-factor and nocodazole efficiently synchronized cultures at the non-budded or large-budded stages, respectively.
source: Treatment with α-factor (Figure 6B) and nocodazole (Figure 6C) efficiently synchronized cultures at the non-budded or large-budded stages, respectively, and did not alter Hsp104 protein levels or localization relative to the asynchronous culture at 30°C (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: Treatment with α-factor and nocodazole did not alter Hsp104 protein levels or localization relative to the asynchronous culture at 30°C.
source: Treatment with α-factor (Figure 6B) and nocodazole (Figure 6C) efficiently synchronized cultures at the non-budded or large-budded stages, respectively, and did not alter Hsp104 protein levels or localization relative to the asynchronous culture at 30°C (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: At 40°C, Hsp104-GFP protein levels increased to similar extents in the asynchronous and arrested cultures.
source: At 40°C, Hsp104-GFP protein levels increased to similar extents in the asynchronous and arrested cultures (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), and its localization to cytoplasmic foci was similar in all cases (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Hsp104-GFP localization to cytoplasmic foci was similar in asynchronous and arrested cultures at 40°C.
source: At 40°C, Hsp104-GFP protein levels increased to similar extents in the asynchronous and arrested cultures (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), and its localization to cytoplasmic foci was similar in all cases (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The distribution of Hsp104-GFP in the α-factor arrested culture remained normal at 40°C.
source: By flow cytometry, the distribution of Hsp104-GFP in the α-factor arrested culture remained normal (Figure 6D), but in the nocodazole-arrested culture, this distribution became bimodal (Figure 6E), indicating that Hsp104-GFP asymmetry is established immediately, even before cell division.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In the nocodazole-arrested culture, the distribution of Hsp104-GFP became bimodal at 40°C.
source: By flow cytometry, the distribution of Hsp104-GFP in the α-factor arrested culture remained normal (Figure 6D), but in the nocodazole-arrested culture, this distribution became bimodal (Figure 6E), indicating that Hsp104-GFP asymmetry is established immediately, even before cell division.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Hsp104-GFP asymmetry is established immediately, even before cell division.
source: By flow cytometry, the distribution of Hsp104-GFP in the α-factor arrested culture remained normal (Figure 6D), but in the nocodazole-arrested culture, this distribution became bimodal (Figure 6E), indicating that Hsp104-GFP asymmetry is established immediately, even before cell division.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Hsp104-GFP distribution becomes bimodal in nocodazole-arrested cells, shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Arrest without exposure to elevated temperature did not induce curing.
source: Arrest, without exposure to elevated temperature, did not induce curing (Figure 6F,G).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6F and 6G.

claim: In α-factor arrested cells, exposure to 40°C at release inefficiently cured [PSI+]Weak (∼15%).
source: In α-factor arrested cells, exposure to 40°C at release inefficiently cured [PSI+]Weak (∼15%; Figure 6F), but in nocodazole-arrested cells, curing was nearly quantitative (∼90%; Figure 6G) consistent with the asymmetric localization of Hsp104-GFP in the latter but not the former case (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: In nocodazole-arrested cells, exposure to 40°C at release resulted in nearly quantitative curing (∼90%).
source: In α-factor arrested cells, exposure to 40°C at release inefficiently cured [PSI+]Weak (∼15%; Figure 6F), but in nocodazole-arrested cells, curing was nearly quantitative (∼90%; Figure 6G) consistent with the asymmetric localization of Hsp104-GFP in the latter but not the former case (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Cells at the end of the cell cycle are more sensitive to curing at elevated temperature than those at the beginning of the cell cycle.
source: These observations suggest that cells at the end of the cell cycle are more sensitive to curing at elevated temperature than those at the beginning of the cell cycle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings shown in Figures 6F and 6G.

claim: For the culture originally arrested with α-factor, sensitivity to curing at elevated temperature increased as cells progressed into the late stages of the cell cycle.
source: To test this idea, we released cultures from arrest and, after 30 min of growth at 30°C, exposed them to 40°C. For the culture originally arrested with α-factor, sensitivity to curing at elevated temperature increased (Figure 6F) as cells progressed into the late stages of the cell cycle (Figure 6B), and for the culture originally arrested with nocodazole, this sensitivity declined (Figure 6G) with cell-cycle progression (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6F and 6B.

claim: For the culture originally arrested with nocodazole, sensitivity to curing declined with cell-cycle progression.
source: To test this idea, we released cultures from arrest and, after 30 min of growth at 30°C, exposed them to 40°C. For the culture originally arrested with α-factor, sensitivity to curing at elevated temperature increased (Figure 6F) as cells progressed into the late stages of the cell cycle (Figure 6B), and for the culture originally arrested with nocodazole, this sensitivity declined (Figure 6G) with cell-cycle progression (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6G and 6C.

claim: Curing occurs most efficiently when cells at a late stage of the cell cycle are exposed to elevated temperature.
source: Thus, curing occurs most efficiently when cells at a late stage of the cell cycle are exposed to elevated temperature.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings shown in Figures 6F and 6G.

claim: Hsp104-GFP retention was significantly reduced at all temperatures when unbudded cells were exposed to elevated temperature in comparison with budded cells.
source: In comparison with budded cells, Hsp104-GFP retention was significantly reduced at all temperatures when unbudded cells were exposed to elevated temperature, but the magnitude of the effect was most severe for conditions that induced curing (30°C→40°C and 37°C→40°C; Figure 5A, orange), indicating a cell-cycle stage dependence on Hsp104-GFP retention at elevated temperature.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Nearly 100% of cells contained Hsp104-GFP foci immediately after thermal stress.
source: Indeed, nearly 100% of cells contained Hsp104-GFP foci immediately after thermal stress (Figure 7A) but only ∼80% still contained foci when cell division re-initiated ∼150 min after incubation at 40°C (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Only ∼80% of cells still contained Hsp104-GFP foci when cell division re-initiated ∼150 min after incubation at 40°C.
source: Indeed, nearly 100% of cells contained Hsp104-GFP foci immediately after thermal stress (Figure 7A) but only ∼80% still contained foci when cell division re-initiated ∼150 min after incubation at 40°C (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: 60% of unbudded cells resolved Hsp104-GFP foci prior to cell division.
source: Consistent with this idea, 60% of unbudded cells, which are inefficiently cured (Figure 6F), resolved Hsp104-GFP foci prior to cell division (Figure 7B [165–210 min], Figure 7C), allowing the partitioning of the chaperone (Figures 7B and 5A, orange).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7B and 7C.

claim: In budded cells, only ∼8% of cells had resolved heat-induced Hsp104-GFP foci by the time the cell divided.
source: In budded cells, which are efficiently cured (Figure 6G), only ∼8% of cells had resolved heat-induced Hsp104-GFP foci by the time the cell divided (Figure 7B [105 min], Figure 7C), leading to the asymmetric retention of Hsp104-GFP (Figures 7B and 5A, gray).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7B and 7C.

claim: Hsp104 is retained in cells exposed to elevated temperature if it is unable to resolve its heat-induced substrates prior to cell division.
source: Together, these observations indicate that Hsp104 is retained in cells exposed to elevated temperature if it is unable to resolve its heat-induced substrates prior to cell division.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings shown in Figures 7B and 7C.

claim: Substrate–chaperone dynamics create a temporal limitation on proteostasis capacity.
source: Because sensitivity to curing at elevated temperature correlated with cell-cycle stage (Figure 6F,G) and Hsp104-GFP localization to these cytoplasmic foci (Figure 5), substrate–chaperone dynamics must create a temporal limitation on proteostasis capacity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings shown in Figures 6F,G and 5.

claim: Expression of the molecular chaperone Hsp104, even at its low basal level, reduces organismal fitness at the normal growth temperature in S. cerevisiae.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, expression of the molecular chaperone Hsp104, even at its low basal level, reduces organismal fitness at the normal growth temperature; however, survival at elevated temperatures is absolutely dependent on Hsp104, whose expression is induced to high levels by heat shock (Sanchez et al., 1992; Escusa-Toret et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Survival at elevated temperatures is absolutely dependent on Hsp104 in S. cerevisiae.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, expression of the molecular chaperone Hsp104, even at its low basal level, reduces organismal fitness at the normal growth temperature; however, survival at elevated temperatures is absolutely dependent on Hsp104, whose expression is induced to high levels by heat shock (Sanchez et al., 1992; Escusa-Toret et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cell-based limitations must finely tune proteostasis capacity to control protein misfolding induced by stress and to allow normal protein folding in the absence of these challenges.
source: Thus, cell-based limitations must finely tune proteostasis capacity not only to control protein misfolding induced by stress but also to allow normal protein folding in the absence of these challenges (Morimoto, 2008).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that Hsp104 expression has different effects at different temperatures, supported by a citation.

claim: The increase in Hsp104 expression at elevated temperature alone is not sufficient to induce Sup35 amyloid resolution and [PSI+]Weak curing.
source: Our studies indicate that the increase in Hsp104 expression at elevated temperature alone is not sufficient to induce Sup35 amyloid resolution and [PSI+]Weak curing (Figures 1, 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: Chaperone spatial engagement, substrate processing dynamics, and partitioning during cell division represent cell based limitations on proteostasis capacity.
source: Thus, chaperone spatial engagement, substrate processing dynamics, and partitioning during cell division represent cell based limitations on proteostasis capacity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented throughout the study.

claim: Metazoans lack an Hsp104 homolog.
source: Metazoans lack an Hsp104 homolog (Torrente and Shorter, 2013), but disaggregase activity has also recently been linked to a multi-component system in yeast comprised of Hsp110, Hsp70, and Hsp40, and this activity is conserved in the C. elegans and human homologs of these chaperones (Shorter, 2011; Rampelt et al., 2012; Mattoo et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Disaggregase activity has been linked to a multi-component system in yeast comprised of Hsp110, Hsp70, and Hsp40.
source: Metazoans lack an Hsp104 homolog (Torrente and Shorter, 2013), but disaggregase activity has also recently been linked to a multi-component system in yeast comprised of Hsp110, Hsp70, and Hsp40, and this activity is conserved in the C. elegans and human homologs of these chaperones (Shorter, 2011; Rampelt et al., 2012; Mattoo et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The disaggregase activity of the Hsp110/Hsp70/Hsp40 system is conserved in the C. elegans and human homologs of these chaperones.
source: Metazoans lack an Hsp104 homolog (Torrente and Shorter, 2013), but disaggregase activity has also recently been linked to a multi-component system in yeast comprised of Hsp110, Hsp70, and Hsp40, and this activity is conserved in the C. elegans and human homologs of these chaperones (Shorter, 2011; Rampelt et al., 2012; Mattoo et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The Hsp110/Hsp70/Hsp40 system is largely ineffective in the disaggregation of amyloid in vitro.
source: This system is largely ineffective in the disaggregation of amyloid in vitro (Shorter, 2011) but can promote the slow disassembly of amyloid from fiber ends in the presence of small heat shock proteins, such as Hsp26 and Hsp42 from yeast or HspB5 from humans (Duennwald et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The Hsp110/Hsp70/Hsp40 system can promote the slow disassembly of amyloid from fiber ends in the presence of small heat shock proteins.
source: This system is largely ineffective in the disaggregation of amyloid in vitro (Shorter, 2011) but can promote the slow disassembly of amyloid from fiber ends in the presence of small heat shock proteins, such as Hsp26 and Hsp42 from yeast or HspB5 from humans (Duennwald et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Hsp110 localizes to foci containing misfolded protein in human cells following thermal stress.
source: Like Hsp104 in yeast, Hsp110 localizes to foci containing misfolded protein in human cells following thermal stress (Rampelt et al., 2012) and interacts with protein amyloids in vivo (Ishihara et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2009; Olzscha et al., 2011), raising the possibility that Hsp110 engagement with stress-induced substrates could also promote its activity toward amyloidogenic substrates in vivo.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Hsp110 interacts with protein amyloids in vivo.
source: Like Hsp104 in yeast, Hsp110 localizes to foci containing misfolded protein in human cells following thermal stress (Rampelt et al., 2012) and interacts with protein amyloids in vivo (Ishihara et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2009; Olzscha et al., 2011), raising the possibility that Hsp110 engagement with stress-induced substrates could also promote its activity toward amyloidogenic substrates in vivo.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Hsp110 engagement with stress-induced substrates could promote its activity toward amyloidogenic substrates in vivo.
source: Like Hsp104 in yeast, Hsp110 localizes to foci containing misfolded protein in human cells following thermal stress (Rampelt et al., 2012) and interacts with protein amyloids in vivo (Ishihara et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2009; Olzscha et al., 2011), raising the possibility that Hsp110 engagement with stress-induced substrates could also promote its activity toward amyloidogenic substrates in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the parallel between Hsp104 in yeast and Hsp110 in humans.

claim: The spatial engagement of PQC factors is a newly appreciated consequence of their function in vivo.
source: The spatial engagement of PQC factors, including both chaperones and components of the ubiquitin–proteasome system, is a newly appreciated consequence of their function in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Numerous cytoplasmic foci arise in response to stressors including heat, aging, oxidation, and/or proteasome inhibition.
source: Numerous cytoplasmic foci arise in response to stressors including heat, aging, oxidation, and/or proteasome inhibition. These foci include aggresomes, the insoluble protein deposit (IPOD), the juxtanuclear quality control compartment (JUNQ), StiF-inducible foci (StiF), and Q-bodies, the latter of which form under the mild thermal stress conditions employed in our studies (Johnston et al., 1998; Erjavec et al., 2007; Kaganovich et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2010; Specht et al., 2011; Malinovska et al., 2012; Weisberg et al., 2012; Escusa-Toret et al., 2013; Wolfe et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Q-bodies form under the mild thermal stress conditions employed in this study.
source: Numerous cytoplasmic foci arise in response to stressors including heat, aging, oxidation, and/or proteasome inhibition. These foci include aggresomes, the insoluble protein deposit (IPOD), the juxtanuclear quality control compartment (JUNQ), StiF-inducible foci (StiF), and Q-bodies, the latter of which form under the mild thermal stress conditions employed in our studies (Johnston et al., 1998; Erjavec et al., 2007; Kaganovich et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2010; Specht et al., 2011; Malinovska et al., 2012; Weisberg et al., 2012; Escusa-Toret et al., 2013; Wolfe et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PQC factors that localize to cytoplasmic foci promote survival under stress.
source: The PQC factors that localize to these foci, such as Hsp104, clearly promote survival under stress (Sanchez et al., 1992; Escusa-Toret et al., 2013), but whether their localization into cytoplasmic foci specifically altered proteostasis capacity had not been previously established.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The engagement of Hsp104 with heat-induced misfolded protein aggregates enhances proteostasis capacity by increasing the accumulation of this factor beyond the level attainable by changes in gene expression.
source: Our studies indicate that the engagement of Hsp104 with heat-induced misfolded protein aggregates enhances proteostasis capacity by increasing the accumulation of this factor beyond the level attainable by changes in gene expression (Figure 5) and thereby permitting the disassembly of existing Sup35 amyloid (Figures 1,5).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings shown in Figures 1 and 5.

claim: The accumulation of protein aggregates has been linked to reduced proteostasis capacity in vivo.
source: Indeed, our observations reveal other cell-based limitations beyond chaperone partitioning. For example, in contrast to the proteostasis enhancement we observe following thermal stress in yeast, previous studies have linked the accumulation of protein aggregates to reduced proteostasis capacity in vivo (Broadley and Hartl, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Protein aggregates resulting from oxidative damage with age or proteotoxic stresses have been linked to reduced replicative lifespan.
source: In these cases, protein aggregates, including those resulting from oxidative damage with age or proteotoxic stresses, have been linked to reduced replicative lifespan, (Aguilaniu et al., 2003; Hernebring et al., 2006; Rujano et al., 2006; Erjavec et al., 2007, 2008; Tessarz et al., 2009; Knorre et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2010; Unal et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2011; Spokoini et al., 2012) and, the presence of protein amyloids, such as polyglutamine-expanded proteins and other yeast prions, promote the misfolding of metastable proteins, interfere with proteolysis, reduce protein synthesis, inhibit endocytosis, and disrupt prion propagation through the sequestration of chaperones (Gidalevitz et al., 2006; Meriin et al., 2003; Kirstein-Miles and Morimoto, 2013; Park et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The presence of protein amyloids promotes the misfolding of metastable proteins, interferes with proteolysis, reduces protein synthesis, inhibits endocytosis, and disrupts prion propagation through the sequestration of chaperones.
source: In these cases, protein aggregates, including those resulting from oxidative damage with age or proteotoxic stresses, have been linked to reduced replicative lifespan, (Aguilaniu et al., 2003; Hernebring et al., 2006; Rujano et al., 2006; Erjavec et al., 2007, 2008; Tessarz et al., 2009; Knorre et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2010; Unal et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2011; Spokoini et al., 2012) and, the presence of protein amyloids, such as polyglutamine-expanded proteins and other yeast prions, promote the misfolding of metastable proteins, interfere with proteolysis, reduce protein synthesis, inhibit endocytosis, and disrupt prion propagation through the sequestration of chaperones (Gidalevitz et al., 2006; Meriin et al., 2003; Kirstein-Miles and Morimoto, 2013; Park et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The dynamics of chaperone engagement with distinct substrates, rather than simply their presence, correlates with the impact of these interactions on proteostasis capacity.
source: A comparison of these studies with our work suggests that the dynamics of chaperone engagement with distinct substrates, rather than simply their presence, correlates with the impact of these interactions on proteostasis capacity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the current study's findings with previous literature.

claim: No differences in Hsp104-GFP localization were detected in [PSI+] and [psi−] strains expressing Sup35 at its endogenous level at 30°C.
source: In contrast, we detect no differences in Hsp104-GFP localization in [PSI+] and [psi−] strains expressing Sup35 at its endogenous level (Figure 4A, 30°C), and Sup35 amyloid can clearly be resolved at these native stoichiometries when the system is elevated to a distinct but accessible proteostatic niche (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Sup35 amyloid can be resolved at native stoichiometries when the system is elevated to a distinct but accessible proteostatic niche.
source: In contrast, we detect no differences in Hsp104-GFP localization in [PSI+] and [psi−] strains expressing Sup35 at its endogenous level (Figure 4A, 30°C), and Sup35 amyloid can clearly be resolved at these native stoichiometries when the system is elevated to a distinct but accessible proteostatic niche (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings shown in Figure 1D.

claim: [PSI+] can transition from a benign to a toxic state upon Sup35 overexpression.
source: However, paralleling the studies in metazoans, [PSI+] can transition from a benign to a toxic state upon Sup35 overexpression (Ter-Avanesyan et al., 1993), a condition that also induces Hsp70 co-localization (Winkler et al., 2012).
